talks.title: SIGINT, COMINT, Hack it
talks.teaser: Surveys radio attack surfaces in cars, garage doors, cellular links and V2G charging, plus low-cost tooling for analysing signals.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's background running a wireless and hardware security firm, and argues that radio now sits behind many everyday systems, from access control and phones to cars. Because radio signals are invisible and often exotic, practitioners need proper instruments rather than consumer gadgets alone, such as a spectrum analyser, a good antenna and software-defined radio hardware. A containerised toolkit that runs across several processor architectures is also presented.

The middle section walks through a workflow: sweep to find an interesting frequency, characterise it with spectrum, waterfall and constellation views, demodulate it, then decode its structure and recover keys where encryption is involved. Examples include tyre pressure sensors, remote keyless entry and rolling codes, garage door programming, FM subcarriers such as RDS and DAB, and a car's Bluetooth link that exposed a Wi-Fi passphrase. Other cases cover GSM downgrades to impersonate a mobile operator, back-end API flaws enabling remote unlocking, and power-line signals leaking from charging cables.

The closing part looks ahead to newer technologies such as V2X and 5G-connected vehicles, where tooling is still immature. The main takeaway is that manufacturers must protect secrets in both firmware and hardware, and that developers who reuse old protocol stacks keep reintroducing known vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Hacking people and organizations for greater good
talks.teaser: Explains how organizational culture, scoping and executive support decide whether security work succeeds in practice.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that culture forms in every group whether or not anyone plans it, and that it can be guided on purpose. To illustrate, the speakers recall a military squad whose strong team identity came from a shared goal, individual incentives and clearly split responsibilities. They describe culture in layers: visible artifacts such as documents, org charts and dress codes, then stated values, and finally unspoken assumptions, which are the hardest to change but last the longest.

The middle section covers common ways security efforts fail. Typical examples include a gap between strategy and daily practice, copying solutions without tailoring them to the context, weak communication, and bringing security in too late, after a project has already moved in the wrong direction. The speakers walk through a set of questions for practitioners: why the program exists, who owns decisions and holds the budget, what "done" and "secure enough" mean, and how tightly the work should be scoped. They suggest that a change in leadership can open a window for new initiatives, and that honest audits and early involvement in planning help security teams gain visibility.

The closing points stress building support from higher management, staying active and collaborative rather than only pointing out faults, and offering solutions alongside findings. The session ends with thanks to the volunteers who run the event and a request for attendees to take their trash with them.

talks.title: State of Union
talks.teaser: Tests upcoming EU rules for connected consumer devices by dismantling popular products sold in Finland.
talks.summary:
The talk tests upcoming European regulation for connected consumer devices against real products instead of only reading the regulatory text. It starts from the Radio Equipment Directive's cybersecurity requirements and the forthcoming Cyber Resilience Act. The research collected 22 best-selling devices in Finland across healthcare, home automation and IP camera categories. Each was dismantled, its firmware dumped and its network behaviour observed. A child-monitoring camera with a companion sensor serves as a detailed case study.

The case study failed several requirements: firmware stored in clear text, a fixed default password, known vulnerabilities, and personal data that remained after the device was wiped through the app. Across the full set, communication encryption was surprisingly strong, with most devices using TLS and certificate pinning and many running without an operating system. The weaker areas were data handling and maintenance. Many products shared data with third parties without an opt-out, many did not delete data on reset, and software updates were rarely enforced for always-connected cameras and home automation gear. Nearly half relied on outsourced development, which made reporting vulnerabilities to engineers difficult.

The main takeaway is that the supply chain, data deletion and update practices need attention beyond transport encryption. The speaker plans to repeat the measurements in a year or two to see whether the regulation changes these results.

talks.title: Guardians of the Hypervisor
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers reach VMware ESXi hosts and run ransomware on them, and which hardening and logging steps counter it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from why VMware vCenter and ESXi are attractive targets for ransomware. vCenter manages every host and virtual machine, and an ESXi host gives direct access to the datastores that hold virtual disks. The speakers, both from an incident response background, note that many intrusions are quiet rather than smash-and-grab, and that attackers like hypervisors because they are poorly monitored.

The middle section covers how intrusions typically happen. The most common route is through Active Directory accounts that hold administrative rights on vCenter. Other routes include passwords saved in browsers or text files, backup application credentials, and vulnerable virtual USB devices in guest machines. A live demo shows an attacker resetting the root password through vCenter and re-enabling SSH despite lockdown mode. The speakers then walk through ESXi ransomware samples, including one that shuts down virtual machines and encrypts VMDK files, and a leaked log showing an operator struggling with the platform's differences from Linux. They also test protective settings such as the exec-installed-only option and the VPX user shell-access restriction, and show how each can be bypassed.

The closing section focuses on defence. Default ESXi and vCenter logs are verbose, so the speakers suggest hunting for specific events such as root logins, configuration changes and ransomware-related messages. They recommend layering architecture, hardening, detection and response, and planning recovery with rebuildable hosts.

talks.title: OODA Loops and Building Mental Snowmobiles
talks.teaser: Explains the OODA loop and decision science, applying Boyd's ideas to incident response and organizational planning.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the OODA loop, a decision model developed by Air Force pilot John Boyd, and places it within decision science. The speaker covers Boyd's background and his influence on the F-15 design after a direct meeting pushed leadership to cancel the F-111 variant project. He also reviews ideas behind his thinking, including Hicks' law on how more options slow decisions, and a range of cognitive biases that distort judgment.

The middle section focuses on practical tools. Decisions are sorted by reversibility and repetition, so routine, reversible choices move down to junior staff while high-stakes, one-shot choices stay with leaders. Two planning methods are presented: MESCA, for scoring courses of action against must-haves and won't-accepts, and PACE, for layering primary, alternate, contingency and emergency plans. Backward planning from a desired future is also covered. Examples include survivorship bias in WWII bomber armor, the railroad-gauge origin of rocket booster width, and the response to the September 11 attacks, used to show how people freeze under stress and why they need to keep moving.

The closing portion applies the loop to cyber work, including automating business rules, running tabletop exercises where outcomes are decided by dice rolls, and tracing anomaly detection from global and contextual methods toward collective analysis. The takeaways are to keep the loop moving, limit the options given to decision makers, build the next generation of leaders, and ask for help when needed.

talks.title: Hunting for Attack Paths in OpenAPI Documentations
talks.teaser: Shows how OpenAPI specifications can be mined as graphs to surface API design flaws like inconsistent authorization and leaked identifiers.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a penetration tester, starts from a practical gap: OpenAPI files describe every endpoint, parameter and data object an API exposes, and they are published in large numbers. Reviewing them by hand is slow, so the research asks whether the specification alone can reveal security design faults before an API is built or tested.

The approach loads the document into a Neo4j graph, with endpoints, methods, objects, fields and security requirements as nodes, then runs queries to find paths between them. Four attack-path ideas are covered: sensitive data reachable through both protected and public endpoints, identifiers that leak in other responses and can be reused, parallel endpoints that could spread data extraction past a per-endpoint rate limit, and fields that are reflected back to users. Nested object references and many optional elements made parsing messy.

Runs against a large corpus of public specifications surfaced a contact-details object that was open on one endpoint and authenticated on another, likely an oversight, and helped locate valid parameter values that would otherwise be guesswork. The closing takeaway is that graph queries can flag likely design mistakes early, which is useful to both defenders and testers, though findings still need manual verification and the prototype is rough.

talks.title: Exploiting Token Based Authentication
talks.teaser: Shows how stolen signing keys and primary refresh tokens let attackers forge logins and bypass MFA in Entra ID.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a refresher on how web authentication has developed, from HTTP authentication schemes to federated single sign-on. It compares Kerberos tickets, SAML assertions and OAuth-style access tokens used with Microsoft Entra ID, including hybrid setups where an on-premises AD FS server vouches for users. The speaker frames the core risk: a bearer token lets whoever holds it act as the user, no matter how strong the original sign-in was.

The middle section covers two attack paths. The first is stealing secrets from the identity provider, such as the AD FS token-signing certificate, which makes it possible to mint tokens that satisfy MFA and conditional access. The second is stealing tokens from a user's managed device, including primary refresh tokens and session keys, which can then be used to request access tokens while presenting a trusted device identity. Live demonstrations walk through both chains. For detection, the speaker recommends correlating identity provider sign-in logs with service-side usage logs, checking unique token identifiers, and comparing the IP address recorded in a token with the address that requested it.

The closing part covers prevention: hardening the identity provider, removing local admin rights from users, and using Entra token protection and continuous access evaluation. These controls reduce the risk but are not complete fixes. The talk ends by discussing a 2023 incident involving an expired consumer signing key and summarises that stolen tokens give temporary access, while stolen secrets give persistent access as any user.

talks.title: Supercharging Your Security Pipeline
talks.teaser: Shows how centralizing vulnerability findings from many security tools in one place cuts noise and speeds up fixes.
talks.summary:
Mikael Nilsson, product security lead for a customer intelligence marketing platform at SAS, explains how his team's development practice moved from waterfall releases to monthly iterations and then to continuous deployment. That change made phased security testing unworkable and pushed scanning into the pipeline. He points to shrinking time-to-exploit figures from a Mandiant report as the reason fixes need to reach production much faster.

The core problem he describes is tool sprawl. Static and dependency scanners, secret scanning, container and cloud posture tools, dynamic testing, bug bounty reports and penetration tests each produce overlapping findings, and sending them straight to developers created duplicate and inconsistent work items. The talk uses DefectDojo, an open-source application security posture management tool, as a reference example of a central place to correlate and deduplicate findings, build an application inventory, triage in bulk and script work through an API. Nilsson stresses that he is not affiliated with the project and is not recommending it over alternatives.

His team now pushes triaged findings into Jira, opens tickets with remediation context, and closes them automatically when a tool stops reporting the issue. Critical exposures on internet-facing services can trigger on-call alerts. The challenges included adopting the central tool late, the developer disruption caused by switching scanners, and heavy Jira customization that forced scripting against the APIs. His practical takeaways are to plan the hierarchy of product types, products, engagements, tests and findings deliberately, and to avoid using Jira for work that is not project management.

talks.title: Adventures in developing a C2 framework
talks.teaser: Traces how a pentest team's remote-access tunnel grew into an in-house command and control framework with custom transports.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how a penetration testing firm's remote-testing setup grew into an in-house command and control framework. It started in 2020, when travel restrictions made internal network tests hard to run. The team built a tool that tunneled UDP over HTTPS so testers could work inside customer networks without firewall changes. During an engagement with strict internal segmentation, that tunnel was repurposed to deliver a shell out to the internet, which pushed the project toward a full C2 framework.

The middle of the talk covers the design. The framework separates connectors, a multiplexer and applications, so new features do not need to handle transport. Supported channels include HTTPS, DNS, ICMP, SMB named pipes, WebSockets, file shares and Gmail drafts. The speaker describes the difficulties of reliable transport, including congestion control and connection teardown bugs. End-to-end encryption uses a TLS 1.2-style handshake with ChaCha20-Poly1305, which the team chose despite the usual advice against rolling your own crypto. Other features include operator-approved staging, in-memory assembly loading in separate AppDomains, Beacon Object File support, and obfuscation and D/Invoke techniques to reduce static detection.

The closing section covers deployment, including a tool that checks implant hashes against VirusTotal to get early warning when defenders upload samples. The main takeaway is that custom tooling can be extended quickly during engagements and helps emulate advanced adversaries, but it demands sustained engineering investment.

talks.title: WarGames: Security in Games
talks.teaser: Explores how game studios face supply chain, server, client, and account threats, from cheating to phishing.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by arguing that game security rests on the same basics as other software security, such as the CIA triad, but differs in data volume, latency requirements and large, passionate player communities. The speakers cover supply chain risk, where attackers can target a studio's tools or hide malware inside a shipped game, and they stress layered defense and good hygiene. Monetization models are discussed as a source of attacker motivation.

The middle section looks at server and client security. Self-hosted multiplayer servers are illustrated with the Minecraft mod ecosystem and a self-replicating worm built for a competition. Client trust is examined through New World item duplication and invisibility bugs, and a Dark Souls remote code execution issue that led to a months-long server shutdown. The speakers also weigh anti-cheat tradeoffs, false positives, DDoS exposure and the physical-world risks of location-based games.

The final part focuses on phishing and account theft, showing how a single character swap in a game's name can mislead players. Detection is described as largely a language problem that needs automation backed by human review. The talk closes by recommending rehearsed incident procedures and gamifying security, such as rewarding players who enable multi-factor authentication, so protection feels like part of play.

talks.title: Will It Run? Fooling EDRs with command lines using empirical data
talks.teaser: Shows how small command-line changes slip past EDR rules, and how a fuzzed model of Windows binaries generates working obfuscations.
talks.summary:
Many intrusions now rely on built-in Windows tools and other trusted executables instead of dropped malware, so defenders increasingly judge intent from the command line. That makes command-line obfuscation attractive: the text changes while the program still runs as intended. The talk starts with simple cases, such as swapping look-alike Unicode dashes past a vendor rule for an encoded PowerShell command, or using unusual slashes and stray characters with a download utility to get past a URL-based rule.

To go beyond one-off tricks, the speaker black-box fuzzed 68 commonly abused Windows binaries and recorded which transformations each one accepted. These included case changes, character substitutions and insertions, dropped trailing characters, alternate path and URL notation, and extra quote marks. Each executable got a JSON model describing its quirks, and a PowerShell module used those models to generate combined obfuscations, which were then checked against real output. Quote insertion worked on about 93 percent of the binaries, and character substitution on about 72 percent.

For defenders, the advice is to stop relying on argument strings alone and to build detections around underlying behaviour in process, file and network events, which are harder to fool. Simple checks, such as unusual quote counts or unexpected Unicode ranges, can also catch many variants. The speaker expects the problem to persist because Windows must stay backward compatible, and notes that macOS and Linux have their own argument quirks, with further research to follow.

talks.title: Flipping Bits: Your Credentials Are Certainly Mine
talks.teaser: Shows how a single flipped bit in a DNS name lets an attacker collect credentials and tokens meant for legitimate services.
talks.summary:
The talk explains bitsquatting, where one bit changes in a domain name held in memory or in transit and turns it into a different name that an attacker can register. The speakers walk through how DNS lookups and TLS handshakes behave when a client ends up at a lookalike host, and why wildcard certificates and long hostnames make the problem harder. They open with a story about a lookalike domain that began receiving email meant for a bank, which led them to look at the technique more closely.

They then describe Certainly, a custom DNS, HTTP and certificate server built to answer for flipped domains. It issues certificates on the fly by completing ACME validation, so clients finish the TLS handshake, and it can log or alter requests and responses, including injecting content into scripts or JSON. Across a test period of about four months, with roughly 25 registered lookalikes for high-traffic services, they recorded tens of millions of DNS requests, a large volume of email, and about two thousand authentication tokens. A hypothesis that solar and cosmic-ray events drive the bit flips was not borne out by their data, so they treated the root cause as an open research question. They also looked at flips in top-level domains.

For defenders, the suggested measures were to register the most likely lookalike domains for priority names, and to restrict outbound connections to expected destinations. They warned that certificate pinning can fail open when it does not account for unknown hostnames, so pinning should be designed to fail closed. The tool was released as open source under the MIT licence.

talks.title: Dissecting the Cicada - In the shadow of the Black Cat
talks.teaser: Traces a Rust-based ESXi ransomware group from a small-company breach back to its affiliate model and forum launch.
talks.summary:
The talk follows an incident response case from autumn 2024, when a small company with fewer than 50 servers was hit by a previously unseen ransomware group calling itself Cicada 3301. The initial access came from brute-forced remote desktop credentials, followed by a remote support tool used for persistence, internal scanning, data exfiltration and encryption. The speakers explain that the Rust-compiled ESXi locker shares a lot with BlackCat, including its key handling, the way it shuts down virtual machines and deletes snapshots, its service and process kill lists, and a Windows safe-mode technique. Infrastructure overlaps and a shared virtual machine image pointed toward a link to the BlackCat operation.

The middle section widens the picture. It covers a remote desktop server that appeared on the same IP address, the timeline of a ransomware-as-a-service launch as seen through forum posts and victim leak sites, and an escrow deposit on a Russian-language cyber crime forum. A developer who advertised Rust malware work was shown receiving a Bitcoin payment, and a password-spraying botnet called Brutus offers a possible source for the initial access. The speakers stress that the evidence is circumstantial rather than conclusive.

The takeaway is a method: combine reverse engineering, infrastructure pivots and forum research into one timeline, because that gives a fuller picture than any single source. The talk also argues that public exposure of these operations can slow a group's recruitment and make it harder for affiliates to trust it.

talks.title: How Fast and Deliberate Swiping Gave Us Access to Very Sensitive Data
talks.teaser: Shows how rapid actions during phone boot slipped past a Samsung kiosk lockdown and reached restricted device functions.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts an internal penetration test for a company that gave field nurses rugged Samsung phones locked down with VMware Workspace One in fully managed mode. Samsung Knox policies blocked Wi-Fi, Bluetooth file transfer and phone settings. Because the phones arrived fully configured, the tester looked at whether the lockdown software itself could be leveraged, rather than only the medical app in scope.

The key observation was timing. While the phone was still booting, before the management launcher's overlay took effect, a few apps could be opened and interacted with. Repeated attempts eventually surfaced Samsung's Edge Panels, a system side menu that stayed usable and kept the launcher paused. With Edge Panels open, the app switcher worked again, so the tester could kill the launcher and remove its permission to draw over other apps. Knox still blocked some features, but Bluetooth restrictions lapsed once the launcher was gone, allowing files to be pulled to a PC, including a system state dump.

The vendor reproduced the issue and worked with Google and Samsung over several months on a fix, which was released with a CVE but not shared with the tester. The speaker suspects Edge Panels is now disabled through Knox policy and that the launcher startup was changed. The practical takeaway is that vendor customizations can open unexpected paths, built-in controls are harder to bypass, and physical devices are preferable to emulators for mobile testing because gestures and hardware buttons behave as in real use.

talks.title: Is this it: Does DevOps development style decrease the security of software?
talks.teaser: Reviews literature on how DevOps practices affect software security and compares the findings with practitioner data.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether adopting DevOps-style development makes software more or less secure. The speaker reviewed academic literature to identify the main security challenges teams face when working this way, and the postures and practices they use to meet them. Many of the listed challenges, such as pipeline security, cloud and microservice complexity, and balancing speed with security, turn out to be general software problems rather than ones specific to DevOps.

The middle of the talk maps the practices onto the four domains of a practitioner maturity framework: governance, intelligence, software development lifecycle touchpoints, and deployment. The academic findings are compared with a practitioner dataset built on the same framework, which shows only a few overlapping practices, such as securing host and network basics and performing security feature reviews. Comparing earlier and later editions of that dataset, the speaker finds that deployment-focused activity has dropped while governance and intelligence work has grown, which is read as progress toward shifting security left.

The speaker concludes that the evidence points toward improvement but is not conclusive, since the data is limited and may be dated. Remaining concerns include the growing number of privileged administrators in development environments and the near absence of training in the reviewed literature. The talk closes by suggesting that AI and low-code platforms may bring the next shift, possibly back toward the deployment side of the lifecycle.

talks.title: Social Engineering and elicitation techniques of hacking a human being
talks.teaser: Walks through social engineering phases, influence tactics, elicitation and physical intrusion examples drawn from red team engagements.
talks.summary:
Dorota Kozlowska, a penetration tester and social engineering specialist, opens with the main social engineering vectors: phishing and spear phishing, watering hole attacks, baiting with infected USB drives, and dumpster diving. She illustrates them with a business email compromise and a county ransomware incident, then walks through four phases: reconnaissance, engagement, exploitation and execution.

Much of the talk covers preparation and psychology. Open-source research, email address format checks, dress codes, and cleaning crews are presented as things to learn before an engagement. She explains empathy and rapport, including how repeated quiet presence in a cafe can make a guard stop seeing an outsider as a threat, and how pretexting changes with the day. She reviews influence principles such as reciprocity, urgency, authority, commitment and social proof, and separates manipulation from persuasion. Elicitation is shown through a conversation built on shared interests, and a staged distraction in a bank lobby illustrates how attention can be redirected.

Physical examples include reaching a server room through an open ceiling, shimming doors, and installing a fake badge reader to collect credentials. She stresses written client consent for documentation, a planned exit, and removing all devices afterward. The closing advice for defenders covers non-committal replies to probing questions, verifying identities, and staff awareness training.

talks.title: Cloud Custodian Unleashed: Automate and Dominate Cloud Governance
talks.teaser: Shows how Cloud Custodian YAML policies report, alert on, and auto-remediate AWS misconfigurations in practice.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why posture scanning and shift-left checks alone leave gaps for a company running many AWS accounts. The speaker describes an environment spanning dozens of accounts and thousands of Terraform resources, where pipeline checks miss emergency changes, infrastructure created outside Terraform, and leaked credentials, and where default posture findings are noisy because they lack business context.

The core of the session is Cloud Custodian, an open-source tool that lets teams write AWS policies in YAML. Live demos cover using it as a query tool that exports non-compliant resources to a CSV report, a continuous alert on newly created security groups through AWS Config, and automated enforcement that re-enables S3 public access blocking within seconds of a change, triggered through CloudTrail, EventBridge and Lambda. A mark-and-sweep pattern is also shown: flag unused security groups with a tag, notify owners, and delete them only after a waiting period has passed.

The practical takeaways are less about the tool than the process. Start by identifying approved "green paths" for common workloads such as static websites, file storage and scheduled data jobs, build standard patterns around them, and deny or migrate deviations. Align policy filters with Terraform so the two do not fight, involve resource owners and agree on response deadlines, and layer controls such as service control policies and origin access controls so one failing feature does not expose the stack. The demo policies and Terraform are published in a repository for anyone to try.

talks.title: Deep fake it till you make it!
talks.teaser: Shows how cheap, off-the-shelf AI tools can clone faces and voices, and why that undermines everyday trust.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a light icebreaker in which the speaker swaps a face in a photo using AI tools, then moves into the history of machine intelligence. It covers a 1984 prediction about synthetic life, Vernor Vinge's idea of the technological singularity, and Nick Bostrom's thinking on risky technologies and a future where AI solves every problem. The core argument is that easy deepfake video and voice cloning together create a dangerous combination.

The middle of the session is a series of live demonstrations using locally run open-source language models and image generators. The speaker builds a fictional tabletop-game character with a matching dating profile, generates portrait images for it, and shows how a single photo can be used to place a face into new poses. He then clones voices from public audio to produce a mock birthday message in the voice of a famous action star and a well-known political figure. With consent, he also clones a volunteer's voice from online recordings to deliver a short message. Some image generation steps did not work well on stage, and the speaker presents this as typical of live demos.

The closing takeaway is that the technology is both exciting and worrying. Listeners should not trust everything they see or hear online, and should pause and verify before acting on unexpected requests, especially ones that appear to come from people they know. Because a few minutes of public video or audio can be enough to build a convincing clone, people should think carefully about what they publish. The speaker ends by reflecting on how one's point of view determines whether the world feels like a utopia or a dystopia.

talks.title: Staying Sneaky in Microsoft Azure
talks.teaser: Shows lesser-known Azure and Entra APIs that enumerate tenants with less logging, and where defenders should add detections.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a tester or attacker can enumerate a Microsoft Entra ID and Azure tenant while avoiding the logs defenders usually watch. The speaker starts from the gap that calls to Microsoft Graph now appear in Graph activity logs, which makes tools such as AzureHound noisy, while some internal, portal-facing APIs do not pass through Graph and leave no comparable record.

He then walks through several of these endpoints. One returns the caller's effective permissions in a single request, another lists users in large batches, and others expose conditional access policies and role assignments for a given user. A clear example involves a privileged group that appeared empty through the standard group query. Querying Privileged Identity Management for groups revealed five eligible members, because just-in-time access hides people who are not currently active.

The closing advice is that this logging gap is a reason to layer detections rather than chase full coverage. Defenders should alert on changes to privileged role assignments and group membership, use endpoint telemetry, restrict access by IP range or managed device, and shorten sign-in frequency and token lifetimes so that stolen sessions must keep being renewed. He also suggests treating the deprecation of Azure AD Graph as a chance to research further undocumented APIs.

talks.title: You're in the Army Now
talks.teaser: Traces how leaked Russian military cyber files expose state-directed operations and what defenders should learn from them.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the argument that technology now changes faster than people and vendors can adapt, and that many products ship with weak built-in security. The speaker, a cyber-physical security specialist, frames the talk around the militarization of cyber operations and uses the leaked Vulcan files as the main case. The material, roughly 100,000 documents and emails from a Russian state technical contractor, was analysed with journalists. It describes military-written requirements for tools covering disinformation, infrastructure disruption, telecom positioning, and operation planning, with a focus on routers, embedded firmware, and undersea cables.

The middle of the talk compares these capabilities with those of the NSA, CIA, Israel's Unit 8200, and the Stuxnet operation, arguing that Russia copied a model other states already use. It traces Russian activity in Ukraine, including the grid disruptions, NotPetya, and the Triton safety-system attack, and argues that these were military-directed rehearsals carried out by civilian contractors who made many operational mistakes. It also notes that civilians can be drawn in as subcontractors, infrastructure, or proxies, and it criticises a Ukrainian volunteer cyber army whose members were pushed into illegal activity.

The closing section argues that defenders need geopolitical and hybrid-warfare awareness, not only indicators of compromise. It points to corporate risk processes, budget cuts for training, and the absence of incident reviews and lessons learned as persistent weaknesses. It suggests governments should warn organisations about activity they see, as the NSA sometimes does, and create incentives for former military cyber staff to move into the private sector.

talks.title: Infostealer - what a menace, man
talks.teaser: Gives an overview of infostealer malware, its service economy, and a rough analysis of leaked credential dumps.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an overview of infostealers, malware that collects saved browser passwords, session cookies, payment cards, wallets and system details from infected machines. It covers common delivery routes such as phishing, fake software, cracked programs and poisoned repositories, and explains how malware-as-a-service operators sell licences, run support channels and push updates to get past new browser protections.

The middle section follows the stolen data into the underground economy. Initial access brokers buy remote access to corporate networks harvested from logs, while marketplaces list victim records by country and infection type. Telegram channels share samples, republish log dumps and offer lookup and cookie-checking services. Examples of operators leaving the market and of fake tools and comment spam used as lures show how quickly the ecosystem shifts.

The closing part describes a rough analysis of large public credential collections. Duplicates were removed and email addresses were matched against registries, bug bounty platforms and cybercrime forums, with some notable overlaps reported. The takeaway is that infostealer logs are useful for account takeover prevention, exposure monitoring and tracking threat actors, but the data is noisy and needs heavy cleaning before any analysis.

talks.title: Investigating Industrial Control Systems
talks.teaser: Walks through how incident responders approach investigating industrial control system environments and the attacks that target them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the role of a national cyber security centre and then establishes the vocabulary of operational technology. It separates OT from IT, distinguishes industrial control systems from SCADA, and explains the Purdue model, which places field devices, PLCs, HMIs and supervisory systems in layers relative to the physical process. Reference architectures from vendors are presented as a starting point for learning which products a site is likely to run.

The middle covers attacks. The speaker walks through an ICS-specific version of the kill chain that separates generic intrusion from a second stage where process-specific impact is engineered. Two campaigns are compared: one that only enumerated industrial networks and one that manipulated Modbus traffic and disrupted heating for apartment buildings. A 2007 lab demonstration of a protective relay being reprogrammed shows how little code can destroy physical equipment, so safety comes first during any response.

On investigation, the speaker contrasts familiar IT practice with ICS realities: heavy legacy, unbacked-up systems, many proprietary protocols, and devices that cannot run endpoint agents. Windows-based engineering workstations and HMIs remain investigable with standard DFIR methods, and much industrial traffic is unencrypted, which helps network-based hunting. The practical takeaway is to reuse an existing process, respect physical safety, and be cautious even with simple scans, since they can disrupt fragile devices.

talks.title: Ten Security Design Strategies from 2004
talks.teaser: Revisits a 2004 internal security training and checks its ten software design principles against today's tooling.
talks.summary:
Camillo Särs revisits an internal security training he built at F-Secure in 2004, walking through its ten principles for designing software that holds up against attackers. He opens with the background of the original deck, which was written for a software engineering team, and sets up the question of what has changed since.

The middle of the talk goes through the principles. He starts with learning from earlier security work, such as 1980s military thinking and the OWASP Top 10, then covers protecting the weakest link, separating duties, and enforcing least privilege with both positive and negative testing. Old Internet Explorer ActiveX problems and an FFmpeg-based thumbnailing service, where untrusted media was treated as hostile, illustrate these points. He also covers defense in depth as time-based protection, never trusting input, failing safely, secure defaults, patching as an ongoing state, dependency management, architectural simplicity, and the limits of asking users security questions. The Thompson "trusting trust" compiler attack serves as a reason to question what you depend on.

The closing section argues that modern frameworks, safe languages, automated dependency checks, immutable ephemeral containers, and short-lived credentials have absorbed many of these lessons. His practical advice is to prioritise the architectural fixes that reduce exposure most, rather than working through long risk spreadsheets, and to be able to explain why each change matters.

talks.title: Playing hide and seek in Java land
talks.teaser: Explores hiding and seeking within Java environments, framed as a playful hide and seek contest.

talks.title: Email hacking, attacks and defence today
talks.teaser: Explains how email authentication standards like SPF, DKIM and DMARC work, and where they fail in practice.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys the current email threat landscape, from the attacks that reach inboxes to the authentication standards meant to stop them. The speaker says spam volume has levelled off while phishing, especially targeted and AI-personalised lures, has become the main problem. Business email compromise and stolen Microsoft 365 logins or session cookies are highlighted as common routes into organisations.

A live demonstration types an SMTP session by hand, showing that the envelope sender and the visible From header are separate things. SPF is judged weak on its own because forwarding and mailing lists break it, and large cloud include records can authorise hundreds of thousands of addresses. DKIM protects message content, yet extra signatures can be attached to unsigned headers unless signed-header lists are enforced. DMARC ties the checks together, but a reject policy can drop legitimate mail. ARC is offered as a way for intermediaries to pass results along.

Practical advice covers senders and receivers alike: sign all outgoing mail with DKIM, publish a DMARC policy, consider DNSSEC for the records, and send bulk mail from separate address ranges. Receivers should not depend on SPF alone, should quarantine suspicious mail rather than block it, and should avoid breaking signatures at forwarding hops. The talk ends by pointing to standards groups and operator working groups as places to follow changes, since email still serves as a fallback identity for many accounts.

talks.title: Navigating Chaos: A Prison's Struggle with Ransomware and Legacy Systems
talks.teaser: Walks through a prison's ransomware breach, from a phishing foothold to a public data leak and the response failures behind it.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a ransomware attack on a prison's IT environment, which ran on decades-old systems with weak patching, no structured incident response plan, and little hardening. A single phishing email, most likely opened by someone in the medical unit, gave attackers a foothold. From there they moved across the network using ordinary techniques such as mapped drives, because segmentation was lacking and nothing monitored the activity. Old documents containing personal data sat in user folders and file shares, and the attackers collected them freely.

The speaker describes how the response made the situation worse. Staff wiped systems instead of preserving evidence, logging was minimal, and backups were encrypted because they were reachable from compromised machines. Warnings from the attackers, including a sample leak and direct contact with the front desk, were ignored. Around 250 GB of data was later published on the dark web, and the talk outlines the resulting legal and compliance fallout under criminal justice and health data rules.

The remedies offered centre on timely patching, a tested response plan, phishing-focused staff training, network segmentation, offline backups and continuous monitoring. The speaker argues that security needs funding and a place at leadership level rather than sitting under facilities management. The takeaway for practitioners is that basic controls could have prevented or limited this breach, and that under-resourced institutions in similar positions can benefit from outside expertise.

talks.title: Web security is fun (or how I stole your Google Drive files)
talks.teaser: Walks through a web security flaw that let an attacker take files from a Google Drive account.

talks.title: Living off Microsoft Copilot
talks.teaser: Shows how prompt injection and poisoned retrieval data can turn Microsoft Copilot into an attack path inside an organization.
talks.summary:
The talk treats Microsoft Copilot as a target inside an enterprise tenant, using illustrative characters such as a CISO, a security engineer and an employee to frame the risk. The speaker explains that the assistant can read far more organizational data than its users see directly, and that sensitivity labels and reference checks do not cover every path. Early attempts to extract data through generated images, arbitrary URLs or code execution were blocked, so the research moved to other inputs.

The central technique is retrieval poisoning. An attacker sends an email or a Teams message from an external tenant that carries hidden instructions and fabricated retrieval snippets. When an employee later asks a routine question, Copilot folds that content into its answer. In the demonstrated case, the answer showed changed bank details while still citing the legitimate source file, which made the manipulation hard to spot. The talk also showed reconnaissance of what the assistant knows, and the generation of convincing spear-phishing emails from existing thread content.

The takeaways are that, for a language model, data effectively becomes instructions, and that jailbreaks are unlikely to disappear. Defenders should treat AI features as experimental, review the references they produce and assume that English-focused safeguards may be uneven. The speaker noted that some requests worked better in other languages, such as Russian.

talks.title: Gateway to Supply Chain Attacks on a Global Scale
talks.teaser: Examines how supply chain attacks can reach a global scale.

talks.title: Out of Order: protocol confusion attacks in the real world
talks.teaser: Shows how skipped protocol steps let an IPMI management service bypass authentication, using reverse engineering, fuzzing and debugging.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces IPMI, the network protocol used by baseboard management controllers to power servers on and off and read sensors independently of their operating system. It explains why these management chips are attractive targets: a compromise sits below the host OS, where endpoint tools cannot see it. Earlier research into weak default ciphers and firmware flaws is recapped as background.

The speaker then outlines protocol security, separating confidentiality and integrity from the application-layer bug classes that matter, such as cryptographic weaknesses, memory corruption and state machine flaws. Practical analysis methods are covered in turn: source review and static scanning, binary reverse engineering, live debugging, and coverage-guided fuzzing, which is awkward for network services. Applied to a software BMC implementation, the review found no checks on message ordering, and debugging showed that session key and privilege data persisted between sessions. Fuzzing turned up only minor memory issues.

Combining these observations produced an authentication bypass. An invalid session left an admin privilege value in memory, and a later session inherited it to send a power-off command without a password. The speaker reports that no instances of this software were found exposed online, and that the issue was reported to the maintainer. The takeaway is to enforce message order and session state at every step, clear session memory when it ends, and treat sequencing as a security property.
